findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, so the scroll-stopping line is buried in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GO SLICES & MAPS: THE FIELD MANUAL. A Go slice is a 24-byte window onto an array you cannot see — and append either writes through that window or silently cuts a new one..."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and demote the series label: "A Go slice is a 24-byte window onto an array you cannot see — and append either writes through that window or silently cuts a new one, depending on capacity nobody at the call site knows about. Part 2 of GO SLICES & MAPS: THE FIELD MANUAL."

findings.summary: The caption advertises slice-mechanics topics that none of Part 2's titles cover, describing what reads as Part 1's content.
findings.evidence: caption: "10 pages on backing arrays, three-index slicing, the 1.18 growth rule, Swiss-table maps in 1.24..." vs. titles: "Map Internals: Swiss Tables & Randomized Range", "Bucket Layout, Overflow & Incremental Growth", "Concurrent Map Access & Slice vs Map Costs", "Operation Costs, Key Rules & Comma-Ok", "Dedupe, Ordered Maps & append Traps", "Buffers That Escape & Pinned Arrays", "Top Mistakes & Field-Tested Rules"
findings.fix: Rewrite the topic list to match the actual pages, e.g. "10 pages on Swiss-table maps in 1.24, bucket layout and incremental growth, why range order is randomized on purpose, concurrent map access, comma-ok and key rules, and the aliasing bugs that only show up in production."

findings.summary: The callout claims the random hash seed is "the direct cause" of unordered map iteration, but iteration randomization is a separate, deliberate runtime mechanism — as the same page later states.
findings.evidence: Callout "Randomly seeded hashing": "The per-process seed defeats hash-flooding denial of service — and is the direct cause of unordered iteration." vs. the later bullet on the same page: "The runtime picks a random start bucket AND a random offset inside it". The seed is also per-map, not per-process: the runtime sets `h.hash0` from a random source at map creation (plus a per-process `hashkey` for aeshash).
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Each map gets its own random hash seed, which defeats hash-flooding denial of service. Iteration order is randomized separately and on purpose — the runtime picks a random start group and slot offset per range statement — so even a fixed seed would not give you a stable order."

findings.summary: The "spec says" table asserts that adding keys repeatedly during a range may never terminate, which neither the Go spec nor the runtime supports.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["add repeatedly", "may never terminate"] under the header "spec says". The spec's map-range paragraph says only: "The iteration order over maps is not specified... If a map entry that has not yet been reached is removed during iteration, the corresponding iteration value will not be produced. If a map entry is created during iteration, that entry may be produced during the iteration or may be skipped." There is no termination caveat, and the iterator is bounded by the table snapshot taken at loop start (`it.buckets`/`it.B` in the pre-1.24 runtime), so the loop always ends.
findings.fix: Replace the row with something true, e.g. ["add repeatedly", "each new entry may or may not be produced"], and retitle the column "spec says" to "behaviour" since the adjacent row ("delete current key" → "fully defined") is also a de-facto guarantee rather than spec text.

findings.summary: Page 1 presents Swiss tables as a replacement for a bucket layout that is not defined until page 2, and uses "buckets" as a load-bearing term throughout before the reader knows what one is.
findings.evidence: Page 1 opens with "Groups of 8 slots plus a SIMD-scannable control word" and "Internal layout changed; language semantics did not", then asserts "clear(m)      // entries gone, buckets stay", "A map that held 1M entries keeps that memory at `len(m) == 0`" and "Delete never gives bucket count back" — while page 2's heading is "Before 1.24: The Bucket Table" with "An array of buckets, each holding up to **8** key/value pairs".
findings.fix: Swap the order: put the page-2 bucket-table section (array of buckets, tophash, overflow, load factor 6.5, incremental growth) first, then present Swiss tables as what replaced it in 1.24, and keep the "Maps Never Shrink" section after buckets have been defined.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: In the map-access flowchart the "no sync needed" box is overlapped by the connector lines running from "reads only"/"any writer" down to "sync.RWMutex"/"sync.Map", with strokes crossing through its text.
findings.evidence: The box labelled "no sync needed" has horizontal/vertical connector strokes drawn straight through the words, and the right-hand connector also cuts through the edge of the "sync.RWMutex" box below it.
findings.fix: Increase the vertical gap between the decision row and the terminal row so the "no sync needed" node sits on its own rank, and route the "any writer" → "sync.RWMutex"/"sync.Map" edges around it instead of through it.

findings.summary: The mutating-while-ranging thread is split across three pages with the entire bucket-internals section wedged into the middle, leaving page 3 to open with three orphaned bullets under no heading.
findings.evidence: Page 1 ends with the "Mutating While Ranging" table (["delete current key","fully defined"], ["add a key","unspecified"]); page 2 opens with the delete-during-range code "if stale(v) { delete(m, k) } // safe idiom" and then immediately switches to "Before 1.24: The Bucket Table"; page 3 then opens with the un-headed bullets "Deleting the current key is the standard filter idiom" and "A new entry may or may not be visited in the same loop".
findings.fix: Move the three range-mutation bullets from the top of page 3 up to sit with the "Mutating While Ranging" table and its filter-idiom code, so the whole iteration-mutation topic closes before the bucket-internals section begins.

findings.summary: Page 4 asserts the nil-map write panic as established fact, but that rule is not stated anywhere until page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 4: "`delete` on a `nil` map is safe too — only writes panic". The first actual statement of the rule is page 5's table row ["zero value","nil, appendable","nil, write panics"] and the bullet "The nil asymmetry is worth memorising: nil slice usable, nil map read-only".
findings.fix: State the nil-map rule where the map basics land — add a line next to the comma-ok code on page 4 such as "reads and `len` work on a nil map; any write panics with `assignment to entry in nil map` — build it with `make` first" — and let page 5's table refer back to it rather than introduce it.

findings.summary: Claims `go vet` catches a discarded `append` result; it does not — the bare-statement form is a compile error and vet has no check for discarded append results.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Ignoring append's return value — the mutation goes nowhere; `go vet` catches it". Writing `append(s, x)` as a statement fails to compile with "append(...) evaluated but not used"; vet's `unusedresult` analyzer covers only functions like `fmt.Sprintf`/`errors.New`, and the `appends` analyzer only flags `append(s)` with no values added.
findings.fix: Change to: "Ignoring append's return value — the compiler rejects a bare `append(s, x)` statement, but assigning to the wrong variable (or `_`) compiles silently and no vet check catches it."
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: Spec sheet 06 renders as an essentially blank page, with one three-bullet section at the top and the remaining ~80% of the page empty grid.
findings.evidence: Page 6 contains only the heading "Buffers That Escape" and three bullets ending at "when the slice outlives the removal"; everything below that (roughly y=470 to y=1440) is empty background.
findings.fix: Merge this section's content into spec sheet 05 or 07, or pull additional blocks forward so the page is filled rather than emitting a near-empty sheet.

findings.summary: The two hardest-to-see slice hazards on page 6 are asserted as bare bullets with no supporting example, including the exact bug the caption sells the post on.
findings.evidence: Page 6's entire body is "Returning a sub-slice of a buffer you will reuse", "Holding a small slice of a huge read and pinning the whole array", "Not nil-ing removed pointer elements when the slice outlives the removal" — while the caption promises "Save it for the next code review where somebody returns `sc.Bytes()`", and `bufio.Scanner.Bytes()` appears nowhere in the part.
findings.fix: Add a code block to page 6 showing the concrete reuse-corruption case — retaining `sc.Bytes()` past the next `sc.Scan()` — with the `bytes.Clone(sc.Bytes())` / `sc.Text()` fix, and a second short block showing a small slice of a 10 MB read pinned until `bytes.Clone` copies it out.

findings.summary: The caption advertises a page count and a topic list that do not match this part's contents.
findings.evidence: Caption: "10 pages on backing arrays, three-index slicing, the 1.18 growth rule, Swiss-table maps in 1.24, why range order is randomized on purpose, and the aliasing bugs that only show up in production" — but this part has 7 slides, and backing arrays, three-index slicing, the 1.18 growth rule and the aliasing chapter are never taught in it.

findings.summary: The pre-ship checklist repeats the false claim that `go vet` reports discarded appends.
findings.evidence: Sidebox "Run before merge": "`go vet` for discarded appends". `go vet` has no analyzer for discarded append results; its `appends` check only reports `append` calls with no values to append.
findings.fix: Change the item to "`go vet` for `append` calls with no values (the `appends` check)", or drop it and keep only the `-race` and presize items.
